P.title: P.blurb
Maths & Logic: Numbers, chance, shapes, statistics and clear thinking.

P.title: ma-numbers.q0.q
Maths & Logic: Which of these is a prime number?

P.title: ma-numbers.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Zero as a number, not just a gap, was developed in India; Brahmagupta wrote rules for it around 628 CE. It reached Europe through Arabic scholars, with Hindu-Arabic numerals.

P.title: ma-numbers.c1.text
Maths & Logic: In 352, the 3 means three hundreds because of its place. Roman numerals had no place value, which made arithmetic painful: try CCCLII × XLVII.

P.title: ma-numbers.c2.text
Maths & Logic: π is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter: about 3.14159. Its digits never end or repeat. Archimedes estimated it around 250 BCE.

P.title: ma-numbers.c3.text
Maths & Logic: A prime has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… Euclid proved around 300 BCE that there are infinitely many.

P.title: ma-numbers.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Multiplying two huge primes is easy; working backwards to find them is extremely hard. RSA encryption, used online, relies on that.

P.title: ma-numbers.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21… It appears in sunflower seed spirals and pine cones.

P.title: ma-numbers.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Square numbers come from multiplying a number by itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Odd numbers add up to them: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

P.title: ma-numbers.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Some infinities are bigger than others. Georg Cantor showed there are more real numbers (all decimals) than whole numbers, even though both are infinite.

P.title: ma-numbers.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Negative numbers were used in China over 2,000 years ago for debts. Europeans resisted them until the 1600s. Today they're on every thermometer and bank statement.

P.title: ma-numbers.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Multiply 9 by any number from 1 to 10 and the digits of the answer add up to 9: 9 × 7 = 63, and 6 + 3 = 9.

P.title: ma-prob.q0.q
Maths & Logic: After 5 heads in a row, the next flip is…

P.title: ma-prob.q1.q
Maths & Logic: In the Monty Hall problem, switching wins…

P.title: ma-prob.q2.q
Maths & Logic: How many people make a shared birthday more likely than not?

P.title: ma-prob.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A fair coin landing heads is 1/2; rolling a six is 1/6.

P.title: ma-prob.c1.text
Maths & Logic: For independent events, multiply for "and": two heads = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Add for "either", if they can't both happen: a 1 or a 2 on a die = 2/6.

P.title: ma-prob.c2.text
Maths & Logic: After five heads in a row, tails isn't "due". Coins have no memory; the next flip is still 50/50.

P.title: ma-prob.c2.viz.items.0.w
Maths & Logic: Red came up 5 times, black is due

P.title: ma-prob.c2.viz.items.0.r
Maths & Logic: Each spin is independent: same odds

P.title: ma-prob.c3.text
Maths & Logic: In a group of just 23 people, there's a better than 50% chance two share a birthday. With 70 people, it's over 99.9%.

P.title: ma-prob.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add. A lottery ticket costing €2 with an expected payout of €1 loses €1 on average.

P.title: ma-prob.c5.text
Maths & Logic: EuroMillions jackpot odds are about 1 in 140 million. You're far more likely to be struck by lightning in your lifetime.

P.title: ma-prob.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Pick one of three doors; the host, who knows, opens a losing door and offers a switch. Switching wins 2/3 of the time. Even mathematicians got it wrong at first.

P.title: ma-prob.c7.text
Maths & Logic: A test is 99% accurate for a disease affecting 1 in 1,000 people. If you test positive, the chance you have it is only about 9%, because false positives from healthy people outnumber true cases.

P.title: ma-prob.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Over a few flips, results can be lopsided. Over thousands, the share of heads gets very close to 50%. Casinos rely on this.

P.title: ma-prob.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Doubles the risk sounds scary, but from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 is a tiny absolute change. Always ask: out of how many?

P.title: ma-geo.q0.q
Maths & Logic: What's the hypotenuse of a triangle with sides 3 and 4?

P.title: ma-geo.q1.q
Maths & Logic: Double the size of a cube: its volume grows…

P.title: ma-geo.c0.text
Maths & Logic: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the longest side equals the sum of the squares on the other two. Builders used 3-4-5 triangles to make square corners.

P.title: ma-geo.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Measure 3 m along one wall and 4 m along the other. If the diagonal is exactly 5 m, the corner is a perfect right angle.

P.title: ma-geo.c2.text
Maths & Logic: The angles in any triangle add up to 180°. Those in a four-sided shape add up to 360°.

P.title: ma-geo.c3.text
Maths & Logic: A circle's area is π times the radius squared. Doubling the radius makes the area four times bigger: why a 40 cm pizza is more than one and a half 30 cm pizzas.

P.title: ma-geo.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Bees build hexagonal cells because hexagons tile a surface with no gaps using the least wall material for the area enclosed.

P.title: ma-geo.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Only five solids have identical regular faces with the same number meeting at each corner: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. Dice use them.

P.title: ma-geo.c6.text
Maths & Logic: A shape has symmetry if a move, such as a reflection or rotation, leaves it looking the same. Snowflakes have six-fold symmetry; your face is roughly mirror-symmetric.

P.title: ma-geo.c7.text
Maths & Logic: If you double the size of an object, its area grows four times and its volume eight times. That's why giant insects couldn't hold themselves up.

P.title: ma-geo.c8.text
Maths & Logic: You can't flatten a sphere without distortion. The Mercator map keeps angles right for navigation but makes Greenland look as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.

P.title: ma-geo.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Fractals repeat their pattern at every scale: coastlines, ferns, broccoli and lightning. Zoom in and you see the same shape again.

P.title: ma-stats.q0.q
Maths & Logic: Which average is best for describing typical salaries?

P.title: ma-stats.q0.x
Maths & Logic: A few very high earners pull the mean up.

P.title: ma-stats.q1.q
Maths & Logic: About what share of values fall within 1 standard deviation in a bell curve?

P.title: ma-stats.c0.text
Maths & Logic: The mean is the average; the median is the middle value; the mode is the most common. They can differ a lot.

P.title: ma-stats.c1.text
Maths & Logic: If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth of the customers shoots up, but the median barely moves. Salaries are better described by the median.

P.title: ma-stats.c2.text
Maths & Logic: Two classes can have the same average but very different spreads. The standard deviation measures how far values typically are from the mean.

P.title: ma-stats.c3.text
Maths & Logic: Many measurements, like heights, cluster around an average in a bell shape. About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation and 95% within two.

P.title: ma-stats.c4.text
Maths & Logic: A well-chosen random sample of 1,000 people can represent millions. A big but biased sample can't: who you ask matters more than how many.

P.title: ma-stats.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Polls report a margin of error. With about 1,000 people it's roughly ±3 percentage points, so 51% vs 49% may be a tie.

P.title: ma-stats.c6.text
Maths & Logic: A chart's y-axis that doesn't start at zero can make a small difference look huge. Always check the scale.

P.title: ma-stats.c6.viz.items.0.r
Maths & Logic: Check the axis: it's a 2% difference

P.title: ma-stats.c7.text
Maths & Logic: A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined. A treatment can look better in each hospital but worse overall, if hospitals have different patient mixes.

P.title: ma-stats.c8.text
Maths & Logic: After an extreme result, the next tends to be closer to average. A sports star's record season is often followed by a more ordinary one, without any curse.

P.title: ma-stats.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Ask four questions: compared with what? Out of how many? Who was measured? Who paid for the study?

P.title: ma-logic.summary
Maths & Logic: Clear thinking, from paradoxes to computers.

P.title: ma-logic.q0.q
Maths & Logic: What is 101 in binary as a normal number?

P.title: ma-logic.q1.q
Maths & Logic: If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is wet. Does it follow that it rained?

P.title: ma-logic.q1.x
Maths & Logic: Something else could have wet it.

P.title: ma-logic.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Logic works with statements that are true or false and combines them with AND, OR and NOT. Every computer chip is built from these operations.

P.title: ma-logic.c0.viz.items.1.b
Maths & Logic: true if at least one true

P.title: ma-logic.c1.text
Maths & Logic: If it rains, the ground is wet doesn't mean "if the ground is wet, it rained": a sprinkler could do that. Confusing the two is a classic logic error.

P.title: ma-logic.c1.viz.items.0.r
Maths & Logic: Something else could have wet it

P.title: ma-logic.c2.text
Maths & Logic: Assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show it leads to nonsense. Euclid proved infinitely many primes this way.

P.title: ma-logic.c3.text
Maths & Logic: This sentence is false. If it's true, it's false; if it's false, it's true. Paradoxes like this shook the foundations of logic in the 20th century.

P.title: ma-logic.c4.text
Maths & Logic: In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent system of rules rich enough for arithmetic has true statements it can't prove. Mathematics can never be complete.

P.title: ma-logic.c5.text
Maths & Logic: An algorithm is a precise step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. The word comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century mathematician in Baghdad.

P.title: ma-logic.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Computers count in base 2, using only 0 and 1. Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…

P.title: ma-logic.c7.text
Maths & Logic: To cross a room, you must first cross half, then half of what's left, forever. Zeno said you'd never arrive. The infinite sum 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … actually equals 1.

P.title: ma-logic.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Some simple-sounding questions remain unsolved, like Goldbach's conjecture: is every even number above 2 the sum of two primes? Tested to huge numbers, never proved.

P.title: ma-logic.c9.text
Maths & Logic: A farmer must cross a river with a wolf, a goat and a cabbage, taking one at a time. The wolf can't be left with the goat, nor the goat with the cabbage. The trick: bring the goat back.

P.title: ma-percent.q0.q
Maths & Logic: A €100 item rises 50%, then falls 50%. What does it cost?

P.title: ma-percent.q1.q
Maths & Logic: A price with 23% VAT is €123. What's the price without VAT?

P.title: ma-percent.q2.q
Maths & Logic: 30% off then 20% off equals a discount of…

P.title: ma-percent.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Per cent means "out of 100". 25% is 25 out of 100, or a quarter. To find a percentage of a number, multiply by the percentage and divide by 100.

P.title: ma-percent.c1.text
Maths & Logic: 10% is easy: move the decimal point one place left. From there, 5% is half of that and 20% is double.

P.title: ma-percent.c2.text
Maths & Logic: 8% of 25 equals 25% of 8, because multiplication works both ways. Use whichever is easier: 4% of 75 is 75% of 4, which is 3.

P.title: ma-percent.c3.text
Maths & Logic: A 50% rise followed by a 50% fall doesn't return you to the start. €100 becomes €150, then €75.

P.title: ma-percent.c4.text
Maths & Logic: If interest rates go from 2% to 3%, that's a rise of 1 percentage point, but a 50% increase in the rate. Headlines often mix them up.

P.title: ma-percent.c5.text
Maths & Logic: A price including 23% VAT is €123. The price before VAT isn't €123 minus 23%; it's €123 ÷ 1.23 = €100.

P.title: ma-percent.c6.text
Maths & Logic: 30% off, plus an extra 20% off is not 50% off. It's 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56 of the price: a 44% discount.

P.title: ma-percent.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Change ÷ original × 100. From 80 to 100 is a 25% rise; from 100 back to 80 is a 20% fall. The starting point matters.

P.title: ma-percent.c8.text
Maths & Logic: To split a €60 bill with a 10% tip among four: €60 × 1.1 = €66, divided by 4 = €16.50 each.

P.title: ma-percent.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Sales up 200%! from 1 to 3 units sounds dramatic but means little. Always ask for the actual numbers behind a percentage.

P.title: ma-fractions.q1.x
Maths & Logic: How many halves fit in three?

P.title: ma-fractions.c0.text
Maths & Logic: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4: three of four equal parts, or 0.75. The bottom number says how many parts; the top says how many you take.

P.title: ma-fractions.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Multiplying top and bottom by the same number doesn't change a fraction: 1/2 = 2/4 = 50/100. Simplify by dividing both by a common factor.

P.title: ma-fractions.c2.text
Maths & Logic: To add fractions, give them the same bottom number first: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

P.title: ma-fractions.c3.text
Maths & Logic: Multiply tops together and bottoms together. Half of three-quarters is 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8. "Of" means multiply.

P.title: ma-fractions.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip. 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6: how many halves fit in 3? Six.

P.title: ma-fractions.c4.viz.items.0.r
Maths & Logic: 3 ÷ ½ = 6, since six halves make three

P.title: ma-fractions.c5.text
Maths & Logic: A ratio compares quantities. A 2:3 mix of cement to sand means 2 parts cement for every 3 of sand: 2/5 of the mix is cement.

P.title: ma-fractions.c6.text
Maths & Logic: A recipe for 4 needs 300 g of flour. For 6 people, multiply by 6/4 = 1.5: 450 g.

P.title: ma-fractions.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Compare deals by price per unit. 500 g for €2.40 is €4.80/kg; 750 g for €3.30 is €4.40/kg. The bigger pack is cheaper here, but not always.

P.title: ma-fractions.c8.text
Maths & Logic: On a 1:25,000 map, 1 cm is 25,000 cm, which is 250 m on the ground. Hiking maps often use this scale.

P.title: ma-fractions.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Twice the hours at the same pay means twice the money: direct proportion. Twice the workers on a job means half the time: inverse proportion, roughly.

P.title: ma-mental.c0.text
Maths & Logic: To add 298 + 157, add 300 and take away 2: 457 − 2 = 455. Rounding to friendly numbers makes many sums easy.

P.title: ma-mental.c1.text
Maths & Logic: To multiply by 5, multiply by 10 and halve. 5 × 48 = 480 ÷ 2 = 240.

P.title: ma-mental.c2.text
Maths & Logic: For a two-digit number, add the digits and put the sum in the middle: 11 × 36 = 3(3+6)6 = 396. If the sum is 10 or more, carry one.

P.title: ma-mental.c3.text
Maths & Logic: To square a number ending in 5, multiply the first part by the next number up and stick 25 on the end: 35² = (3 × 4) then 25 = 1,225.

P.title: ma-mental.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Halve one number and double the other: the product stays the same. 16 × 25 = 8 × 50 = 4 × 100 = 400.

P.title: ma-mental.c6.text
Maths & Logic: A number divides by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3; by 9 if they add up to a multiple of 9; by 4 if its last two digits do.

P.title: ma-mental.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Before calculating, estimate. 49 × 21 is about 50 × 20 = 1,000; if your answer is 10,290, something went wrong.

P.title: ma-mental.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Shopkeepers give change by counting up. Paying €20 for €13.65: up to €14 is 35 cents, up to €20 is €6, so €6.35.

P.title: ma-mental.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Rough Celsius to Fahrenheit: double and add 30. 20 °C ≈ 70 °F (exactly 68). For the exact value, multiply by 1.8 and add 32.

P.title: ma-algebra.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Algebra uses letters for numbers we don't know yet. "A number plus 5 is 12" becomes x + 5 = 12, so x = 7.

P.title: ma-algebra.c1.text
Maths & Logic: An equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Subtract 5 from both sides of x + 5 = 12 to get x = 7.

P.title: ma-algebra.c2.text
Maths & Logic: 3x + 4 = 19: subtract 4 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both by 3 (x = 5). Undo operations in reverse order.

P.title: ma-algebra.c3.text
Maths & Logic: The word "algebra" comes from *al-jabr*, "restoring", in the title of al-Khwarizmi's 9th-century book in Baghdad. Letters for unknowns came later, with François Viète in the 1590s.

P.title: ma-algebra.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Every formula is algebra: area = length × width, speed = distance ÷ time. Rearranging lets you find any missing piece.

P.title: ma-algebra.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Multiply everything inside by what's outside: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. Handy for mental maths too: 3 × 104 = 300 + 12.

P.title: ma-algebra.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Two coffees and a cake cost €5; one coffee and a cake cost €3.50. Subtract: one coffee is €1.50, so the cake is €2. That's a system of equations.

P.title: ma-algebra.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Subtracting a negative is adding: 5 − (−3) = 8. Multiplying two negatives gives a positive: (−2) × (−3) = 6.

P.title: ma-algebra.c8.text
Maths & Logic: In 3, 5, 7, 9…, each term is 2n + 1. Find the 100th term without listing: 2 × 100 + 1 = 201.

P.title: ma-algebra.c9.text
Maths & Logic: A phone plan costs €10 a month plus €0.05 per MB. With €15 a month, how many MB? 10 + 0.05m = 15, so m = 100 MB.

P.title: ma-growth.q0.q
Maths & Logic: A pond is fully covered on day 30, doubling daily. When was it half covered?

P.title: ma-growth.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Linear growth adds the same amount each step; exponential growth multiplies. Exponential starts slow and then explodes.

P.title: ma-growth.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Put 1 grain of rice on the first square, 2 on the next, 4, 8… By square 64, you'd need about 18 quintillion grains, far more than all rice ever grown.

P.title: ma-growth.c2.text
Maths & Logic: Lilies double daily and cover a pond on day 30. When was it half covered? Day 29. Exponential problems look small until the very end.

P.title: ma-growth.c3.text
Maths & Logic: 2⁵ means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Powers are a shorthand for repeated multiplication. Any number to the power 0 is 1.

P.title: ma-growth.c4.text
Maths & Logic: A logarithm asks: "what power?" log₁₀ 1,000 = 3, because 10³ = 1,000. Logs turn huge multiplications into simple additions.

P.title: ma-growth.c5.text
Maths & Logic: The Richter-type earthquake scale, decibels and pH all use logs. Each step up in magnitude means about 32 times more energy released.

P.title: ma-growth.c6.text
Maths & Logic: If each infected person infects 2 others every few days, cases double. Bringing that number below 1 makes an epidemic shrink.

P.title: ma-growth.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Gordon Moore noticed in 1965 that the number of transistors on chips doubled about every two years. It held for decades, powering the digital revolution.

P.title: ma-growth.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Radioactive substances decay exponentially. After one half-life, half remains; after two, a quarter. Carbon-14's half-life of 5,730 years lets us date ancient remains.

P.title: ma-growth.c9.text
Maths & Logic: A sheet of paper about 0.1 mm thick folded 42 times would be over 400,000 km thick, past the Moon. In practice, you can't fold paper more than about 7 times by hand.

P.title: ma-functions.q0.q
Maths & Logic: In y = mx + c, what does m tell you?

P.title: ma-functions.q1.q
Maths & Logic: What shape does y = x² make?

P.title: ma-functions.q2.q
Maths & Logic: On a distance–time graph, the slope shows…

P.title: ma-functions.c0.text
Maths & Logic: A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output, like a machine: put in 3, the rule "double it" gives 6.

P.title: ma-functions.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Descartes' idea: describe any point by two numbers, (x, y): how far across and how far up. It joined algebra and geometry.

P.title: ma-functions.c2.text
Maths & Logic: y = mx + c draws a straight line: m is the slope (how steep), c is where it crosses the y-axis.

P.title: ma-functions.c3.text
Maths & Logic: A taxi charges €3.50 to start plus €1.20 per km. Fare = 1.2 × km + 3.5: a straight line. 10 km costs €15.50.

P.title: ma-functions.c4.text
Maths & Logic: The slope is a rate of change: euros per km, km per hour, degrees per minute. Steeper lines mean faster change.

P.title: ma-functions.c5.text
Maths & Logic: y = x² makes a U-shaped curve called a parabola. A ball thrown in the air follows one, and satellite dishes use its shape to focus signals.

P.title: ma-functions.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Before reading a graph, check what each axis shows, the units and the scale. Then look at the overall shape before the details.

P.title: ma-functions.c6.viz.items.2
Maths & Logic: Does the axis start at zero?

P.title: ma-functions.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Lines show steady change; upward curves show acceleration; curves that level off show saturation, like a phone battery charging.

P.title: ma-functions.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Some quantities move in opposite directions: travel time falls as speed rises. The graph curves down without ever reaching zero.

P.title: ma-functions.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Spreadsheets and programs are full of functions: =SUM(), =AVERAGE(). Each takes inputs and returns one output, exactly like the maths.

P.title: ma-games.q0.q
Maths & Logic: In the prisoner's dilemma, what usually happens?

P.title: ma-games.q0.o1
Maths & Logic: Both betray and are worse off

P.title: ma-games.q1.q
Maths & Logic: Which strategy did well in Axelrod's tournaments?

P.title: ma-games.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Game theory studies decisions where your best choice depends on what others do: business, politics, biology, even crossing the road.

P.title: ma-games.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Two suspects can stay silent or betray each other. Betraying is better for each individually, yet if both betray, both end up worse off than if both had stayed silent.

P.title: ma-games.c2.text
Maths & Logic: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where nobody gains by changing their choice alone. John Nash, subject of *A Beautiful Mind*, defined it in 1950.

P.title: ma-games.c3.text
Maths & Logic: When the game repeats, cooperation can win. In Robert Axelrod's 1980s computer tournaments, "tit for tat" (cooperate first, then copy the other) did remarkably well.

P.title: ma-games.c4.text
Maths & Logic: In zero-sum games, one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, like poker or chess. Most of life, including trade, isn't zero-sum: both sides can gain.

P.title: ma-games.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Two drivers speed towards each other; whoever swerves loses face, but if neither swerves, both crash. It models stand-offs between countries or companies.

P.title: ma-games.c6.text
Maths & Logic: In some games, moving first lets you commit and shape the outcome. In others, waiting lets you learn from the leader's mistakes.

P.title: ma-games.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Game theory designs auctions for radio spectrum worth billions. In a sealed second-price auction, the best strategy is to bid exactly what it's worth to you.

P.title: ma-games.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Animals "play" strategies shaped by evolution: hawks fight, doves share. A mix of both can be stable in a population.

P.title: ma-games.c9.text
Maths & Logic: When a group splits a restaurant bill equally, everyone is tempted to order more, since others share the cost. Everyone ends up paying more: a small tragedy of the commons.

P.title: ma-codes.summary
Maths & Logic: Secret messages from Caesar to your phone.

P.title: ma-codes.q0.x
Maths & Logic: E is the most common letter in English.

P.title: ma-codes.q1.q
Maths & Logic: In public-key cryptography, which key do you keep secret?

P.title: ma-codes.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Julius Caesar shifted each letter three places: A becomes D, B becomes E. Easy to use, and easy to break.

P.title: ma-codes.c1.text
Maths & Logic: In English, E is the most common letter, followed by T and A. Count letters in a coded message and you can guess the substitution. Al-Kindi described this in the 9th century.

P.title: ma-codes.c2.text
Maths & Logic: The Vigenère cipher uses a keyword to shift each letter by a different amount, defeating simple frequency counts. It was called "the indecipherable cipher" for 300 years.

P.title: ma-codes.c3.text
Maths & Logic: Germany's Enigma machine used rotors to change the cipher with every key press. Polish mathematicians first cracked it; Alan Turing's team at Bletchley Park broke it at scale.

P.title: ma-codes.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Modern encryption is public: the method is known, and security comes entirely from a secret key. A 128-bit key has trillions of times more combinations than there are grains of sand on Earth.

P.title: ma-codes.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Your phone uses two keys: a public one anyone can use to lock a message, and a private one only you have to unlock it. Invented in the 1970s.

P.title: ma-codes.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Send someone an open padlock: they lock a box with it, and only you have the key. Nobody needed to share a secret beforehand.

P.title: ma-codes.c7.text
Maths & Logic: A hash turns any data into a fixed-length fingerprint. Change one letter and the hash changes completely. Websites store password hashes, not passwords.

P.title: ma-codes.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Length beats complexity. Four random words are easier to remember and harder to crack than "P@ssw0rd1". Use a password manager and two-factor authentication.

P.title: ma-codes.c8.viz.items.0.r
Maths & Logic: four random words, plus a password manager

P.title: ma-codes.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Large quantum computers could one day break today's public-key systems. New "post-quantum" algorithms were standardised in 2024 to prepare.

P.title: ma-greats.q0.q
Maths & Logic: How did young Gauss sum 1 to 100?

P.title: ma-greats.q1.q
Maths & Logic: Who wrote the first published computer program?

P.title: ma-greats.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Around 300 BCE Euclid wrote *Elements*, building geometry from a few basic axioms. It was used as a textbook for over 2,000 years.

P.title: ma-greats.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Archimedes estimated π, worked out volumes of spheres, explained levers and buoyancy, and supposedly shouted "Eureka!" in his bath.

P.title: ma-greats.c2.text
Maths & Logic: Hypatia of Alexandria (c. 360–415 CE) was a mathematician, astronomer and teacher, one of the first women in maths we know by name.

P.title: ma-greats.c3.text
Maths & Logic: Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, popularised Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe in 1202 with his *Liber Abaci*, a book for merchants.

P.title: ma-greats.c4.text
Maths & Logic: In the 1600s both linked algebra and geometry with coordinates. Fermat also left a famous "last theorem", unproved for 358 years.

P.title: ma-greats.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Both invented calculus independently in the late 1600s and argued bitterly about who was first. We use Leibniz's notation today.

P.title: ma-greats.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Leonhard Euler was the most prolific mathematician ever, writing over 800 papers even after going blind. His identity e^iπ + 1 = 0 links five key numbers.

P.title: ma-greats.c7.text
Maths & Logic: As a boy, Gauss supposedly summed 1 to 100 in seconds: pair 1+100, 2+99… into 50 pairs of 101, giving 5,050.

P.title: ma-greats.c8.text
Maths & Logic: In 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote what's considered the first computer program, for Babbage's Analytical Engine, and foresaw computers making music.

P.title: ma-greats.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Emmy Noether linked symmetry and conservation laws; Ramanujan found startling formulas with little formal training; Maryam Mirzakhani was the first woman to win the Fields Medal, in 2014.

P.title: ma-calculus.q0.q
Maths & Logic: On a speed–time graph, what does the area under the curve give?

P.title: ma-calculus.q1.q
Maths & Logic: At the top of a smooth curve, the slope is…

P.title: ma-calculus.q1.x
Maths & Logic: Peaks and valleys have zero slope.

P.title: ma-calculus.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Calculus answers two questions: how fast is something changing right now (derivatives), and how much has built up over time (integrals).

P.title: ma-calculus.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Your car's speedometer shows speed at an instant, not an average. Calculus defines it by measuring over shorter and shorter time intervals.

P.title: ma-calculus.c2.text
Maths & Logic: A derivative is the slope of a curve at a point: zoom in far enough and any smooth curve looks like a straight line.

P.title: ma-calculus.c3.text
Maths & Logic: An integral adds up tiny slices. On a speed–time graph, the area under the curve is the distance travelled.

P.title: ma-calculus.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Differentiation and integration undo each other: the fundamental theorem of calculus. Distance → speed → acceleration, and back again.

P.title: ma-calculus.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Where a curve peaks or dips, its slope is zero. That's how engineers find the strongest beam or cheapest design.

P.title: ma-calculus.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Cut squares from a 30 cm card's corners and fold up a box. Calculus shows 5 cm squares give the largest volume: 2,000 cm³.

P.title: ma-calculus.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Calculus models population growth, heating and cooling, interest, rocket trajectories and machine learning, which uses derivatives to adjust its weights.

P.title: ma-calculus.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Calculus rests on limits: what a value approaches as something gets very small. 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8… approaches 1, even though no step reaches it.

P.title: ma-calculus.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Newton and Leibniz developed calculus independently in the 1660s–1680s, though Archimedes and others had used similar ideas centuries earlier.

P.title: ma-networks.q0.q
Maths & Logic: Who founded graph theory with the Königsberg bridges?

P.title: ma-networks.q1.q
Maths & Logic: How many colours are enough to colour any map?

P.title: ma-networks.q2.x
Maths & Logic: Links from important pages count more.

P.title: ma-networks.c0.text
Maths & Logic: In 1736 Euler proved you couldn't walk across all seven bridges of Königsberg exactly once. To solve it, he reduced the city to dots and lines: graph theory was born.

P.title: ma-networks.c1.text
Maths & Logic: A graph is a set of nodes (dots) joined by edges (lines). Cities and roads, people and friendships, web pages and links are all graphs.

P.title: ma-networks.c2.text
Maths & Logic: You can trace a network using every edge once only if zero or two nodes have an odd number of edges. Königsberg had four odd nodes.

P.title: ma-networks.c3.text
Maths & Logic: Your map app finds the fastest route with algorithms like Dijkstra's (1956), which explores outward from the start, always extending the shortest path found so far.

P.title: ma-networks.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Find the shortest route visiting every city once. Easy for 5 cities, but the possibilities explode: 20 cities have over 60 quadrillion routes.

P.title: ma-networks.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Stanley Milgram's 1967 experiment suggested any two Americans are linked by about six acquaintances. Facebook data later found an average of about 3.5 steps.

P.title: ma-networks.c6.text
Maths & Logic: In many networks a few hubs have huge numbers of links: major airports, popular websites, influencers. Attack the hubs and the network breaks.

P.title: ma-networks.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Any map can be coloured with just four colours so no neighbouring regions match. Proved in 1976, it was the first major proof that relied on a computer.

P.title: ma-networks.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Google's original idea: a page is important if important pages link to it. It treats the web as a giant graph of votes.

P.title: ma-networks.c8.viz.steps.2
Maths & Logic: Votes from important pages count more

P.title: ma-networks.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Diseases spread along contact networks. Vaccinating well-connected hubs, like healthcare workers, can protect far more people than random vaccination.

P.title: ma-estimate.q0.q
Maths & Logic: How long is a billion seconds?

P.title: ma-estimate.q0.x
Maths & Logic: A million seconds is about 11.5 days.

P.title: ma-estimate.q1.o1
Maths & Logic: A rough estimate built from simple guesses

P.title: ma-estimate.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Physicist Enrico Fermi loved questions like "how many piano tuners are in Chicago?" Break them into pieces you can guess, multiply, and you'll often be within a factor of a few.

P.title: ma-estimate.c1.text
Maths & Logic: About 10 million people, roughly 5 million cars, each filling up weekly: 5 million fills a week. If a station handles about 3,000 a week, that's around 1,700 stations; the real number is a few thousand.

P.title: ma-estimate.c2.text
Maths & Logic: Often the power of 10 matters more than the exact value. Is it hundreds, thousands or millions? Get that right first.

P.title: ma-estimate.c3.text
Maths & Logic: Memorise a few reference numbers and you can estimate almost anything.

P.title: ma-estimate.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Round to numbers that are easy to multiply. 47 × 213 ≈ 50 × 200 = 10,000. The real answer is 10,011.

P.title: ma-estimate.c5.text
Maths & Logic: In multi-step estimates, rounding errors in different directions tend to cancel, so the final answer is often better than any single guess.

P.title: ma-estimate.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Estimation catches mistakes. If a spreadsheet says a café uses 40 tonnes of coffee a day, a quick estimate shows something's wrong.

P.title: ma-estimate.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Count the people in a small area, then multiply by how many such areas the crowd covers. Police and organisers often disagree by a factor of two.

P.title: ma-estimate.c8.title
Maths & Logic: How long is a billion seconds?

P.title: ma-estimate.c8.text
Maths & Logic: A million seconds is about 11.5 days. A billion seconds is about 32 years. Big numbers are very different even if they sound similar.

P.title: ma-estimate.c9.text
Maths & Logic: Good estimators give ranges: "between 2,000 and 4,000". A range you're 90% sure about is more honest than a single precise-looking number.

P.title: ma-patterns.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Add the same number each time: 3, 7, 11, 15… (add 4). The nth term is easy to find: 4n − 1.

P.title: ma-patterns.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Multiply by the same number each time: 2, 6, 18, 54… (×3). They grow much faster than arithmetic sequences.

P.title: ma-patterns.c2.text
Maths & Logic: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15: the number of dots in growing triangles, like bowling pins. The nth is n(n + 1)/2.

P.title: ma-patterns.c3.text
Maths & Logic: Many sunflowers have 34 and 55 spirals; pine cones show 8 and 13. These Fibonacci numbers pack seeds efficiently.

P.title: ma-patterns.c4.text
Maths & Logic: Divide each Fibonacci number by the one before and you approach 1.618…, the golden ratio φ.

P.title: ma-patterns.c5.text
Maths & Logic: Each number is the sum of the two above it. The triangle hides counting numbers, triangular numbers, powers of 2 and probabilities of coin tosses.

P.title: ma-patterns.c6.text
Maths & Logic: Primes thin out but never stop, and no simple formula produces them all. Predicting them is one of maths' deepest open problems.

P.title: ma-patterns.c7.text
Maths & Logic: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… seems obvious, but cut a circle with lines between points and you get 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, then 31. Patterns need proof.

P.title: ma-patterns.c8.text
Maths & Logic: 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221… Each term describes the last aloud: "one 1", "two 1s", "one 2, one 1". A pattern based on words, not arithmetic.

P.title: ma-patterns.c9.text
Maths & Logic: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26… The gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9: odd numbers. The rule is n² + 1.

P.title: ma-units.summary
Maths & Logic: Metres, kilos and why they matter.

P.title: ma-units.q1.q
Maths & Logic: Why was the Mars Climate Orbiter lost in 1999?

P.title: ma-units.q1.o1
Maths & Logic: A mix-up of imperial and metric units

P.title: ma-units.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Born in revolutionary France in the 1790s, the metric system uses powers of 10, so converting is just moving the decimal point. Portugal adopted it in 1852.

P.title: ma-units.c1.text
Maths & Logic: All measurements are built from seven SI base units. Since 2019, all are defined by fixed constants of nature, not physical objects.

P.title: ma-units.c2.text
Maths & Logic: For 130 years the kilogram was a metal cylinder in a vault near Paris. In 2019 it was redefined using the Planck constant.

P.title: ma-units.c3.text
Maths & Logic: 1 m² is 10,000 cm², not 100. 1 m³ is 1,000 litres. Units square and cube along with the lengths.

P.title: ma-units.c4.text
Maths & Logic: A hectare is 100 m × 100 m = 10,000 m², about one and a half football pitches. Farms and forests are measured in hectares.

P.title: ma-units.c5.text
Maths & Logic: The UK and USA still use miles, pounds and Fahrenheit. Quick conversions: 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 lb, 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

P.title: ma-units.c6.text
Maths & Logic: In 1999 a NASA probe was lost at Mars because one team used pound-force and another newtons. The $125 million mistake was a units mix-up.

P.title: ma-units.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Precision should match the measurement. A room measured as 4.2 m doesn't have an area of 17.64 m² precisely; say about 17.6 m².

P.title: ma-units.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Divide km/h by 3.6 for metres per second. 120 km/h is about 33 m/s: a car covers a football pitch every three seconds.

P.title: ma-units.c9.text
Maths & Logic: A kilowatt-hour runs a 1,000 W heater for an hour. A food Calorie is 1,000 calories, about 4.2 kJ. A hot shower uses about 2–3 kWh.

P.title: ma-puzzles.q0.q
Maths & Logic: How many handshakes when 10 people all shake hands once?

P.title: ma-puzzles.c0.text
Maths & Logic: Move a stack of discs to another peg, one at a time, never placing a bigger disc on a smaller one. With n discs it takes 2ⁿ − 1 moves.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c1.text
Maths & Logic: Rearranging four pieces of a triangle seems to create a hole. The trick: the "hypotenuses" aren't straight lines, so the shapes differ slightly.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c1.viz.items.0.r
Maths & Logic: The edges are slightly bent: the shapes aren't equal

P.title: ma-puzzles.c2.text
Maths & Logic: If 10 people all shake hands once, how many handshakes? Each shakes 9 hands, but each handshake involves two: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c3.text
Maths & Logic: If you put 13 socks into 12 drawers, at least one drawer gets two. Simple but powerful: in Lisbon, at least two people have exactly the same number of hairs on their head.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c3.viz.steps.1
Maths & Logic: At least one box has two

P.title: ma-puzzles.c4.text
Maths & Logic: 0.999… repeating forever equals exactly 1. One proof: 1/3 = 0.333…, so 3 × 1/3 = 0.999… = 1.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c5.text
Maths & Logic: A hotel with infinitely many rooms is full. A new guest arrives: move everyone from room n to room n + 1, and room 1 is free. Infinity behaves strangely.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c6.text
Maths & Logic: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Ask either "what would the other say?" and you can reverse the answer to find the truth.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c7.text
Maths & Logic: Sudoku needs no arithmetic, only logic: each row, column and box contains 1 to 9 once. A well-made puzzle has exactly one solution.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c8.text
Maths & Logic: Euler's idea is used in garbage collection and postal routes: planning paths that cover every street once with as little doubling back as possible.

P.title: ma-puzzles.c9.title
Maths & Logic: The wolf, goat and cabbage, solved

P.title: ma-puzzles.c9.text
Maths & Logic: The key insight was taking something back. Many puzzles need a step that seems to go backwards, a lesson for real problem-solving too.
